defaults.permitted_development: A dropped kerb or new vehicular crossing in Wales is not just a driveway surfacing issue. You normally need the highway authority's approval to cross a public footway or verge, and planning permission may also be required where the access serves a classified road or the property has no permitted development rights.

rules.height_rules: No separate height allowance applies. Kerb construction follows highway design standards rather than householder height rules.
rules.depth_rules: There is no national planning depth limit. The council will look instead at the width and depth needed to get a vehicle on and off the highway safely without overhanging the footway.
rules.boundary_rules: The crossing remains part of the public highway. Approval does not give exclusive parking rights on the road, and works must not interfere with utilities, street trees, signs or drainage.
rules.roof_rules: Dropped-kerb works have no roof element. The nearest equivalent design issue is how gradients, retaining edges and any related gateway or canopy are handled, because those parts may be assessed separately.
rules.materials_rules: The highway authority usually specifies the kerb and footway construction, so the main material choice sits in the private driveway behind it. Use durable, well-drained surfacing rather than finishes that shed water onto the pavement or fail under vehicle loading.

restrictions.conservation_area: Creating a vehicular opening through a traditional frontage in a conservation area can need fuller planning scrutiny, especially where walls, railings, paving or trees contribute to the street character.
restrictions.listed_building: A new access serving a listed building or its curtilage can affect historic walls, gates and setting, so listed building consent as well as planning or highways approval may be required.

rules.permitted_development: A dropped kerb or new vehicular crossing in Wales is not just a driveway surfacing issue. You normally need the highway authority's approval to cross a public footway or verge, and planning permission may also be required where the access serves a classified road or the property has no permitted development rights.

rules.height_rules: No separate height allowance applies. Kerb construction follows highway design standards rather than householder height rules.
rules.depth_rules: There is no national planning depth limit. The council will look instead at the width and depth needed to get a vehicle on and off the highway safely without overhanging the footway.
rules.boundary_rules: The crossing remains part of the public highway. Approval does not give exclusive parking rights on the road, and works must not interfere with utilities, street trees, signs or drainage.
